# Debugging ilike {#debugging}

ilike is currently in an early stage of development, and as such, it is likely that you will encounter errors. This section provides some guidance on how to debug these errors. I am working on providing more descriptive error messages where possible.

## Error in ... could not find function ...

Example error:

`Error in get_data() : could not find function "get_data"`

Possible cause:

The compiled ilike model was expecting an R (or Python, or Julia) function named `get_data` to be available to call, but it didn't find it.

Action:

Define the `get_data` function in an `r` (or `py`, `jl`) section of the ilike file, or in a file imported with `import "helpers.R" as helpers` (section \@ref(code-sections)). For a file in the earlier format (appendix \@ref(old-format)), the function goes in a file with the same name as the ilike file (with the extension `.R`, `.py` or `.jl`) in the same directory.

## Parameter index does not correspond to ... in the parameters file

Example error:

...

Action:

...


## Parameters operator variable ... not found in Parameters

Example error:

`Parameters::operator[]: variable 'x' not found in Parameters.`

Possible cause:

Either:

- the Parameters (or Data) object passed into the function does not contain the variable "x";

or:

- the arguments supplied to the function are in a different order to that specified in the documentation. For example, a log likelihood requires the arguments in the order `Parameters`, then `Data` (section \@ref(signatures)), but you may have supplied them in the reverse order.

Action:

Check the order of your arguments, and ensure that the desired variable is correctly referred to in your function.

## cpp::f (used as …): …

Example error:

`cpp::log_likelihood (used as evaluate_log_likelihood): it has arguments (const Parameters &parameters), but a evaluate_log_likelihood function must have arguments (const Parameters &parameters, const Data &data). …`

Possible cause:

The C++ function does not have the signature required by the place where it is used.

Action:

Change the function's arguments (and return type) to those in the message; section \@ref(signatures) lists the signature for each use.

## cpp::f is not defined in a cpp section

Possible cause:

The file uses `cpp::f`, but no `cpp` section of the files being compiled defines a function called `f`; often a misspelt name, or a file left out of `compile()`.

## The constant … is used in the model statements, so its value is needed when compiling

Possible cause:

A constant without a default is used in a model statement (or a move on elements, or a call to another language), whose code is generated when compiling.

Action:

Give the constant a default in the constants section, or give its value to `compile(…, model_parameter_list = list(name = value))` (section \@ref(constants)).

## The constant … was fixed when the recipe was compiled

Possible cause:

The run gives a constant a value different from the one it had when the recipe was compiled, but the constant is used in model statements, moves on elements or calls to other languages, whose code was generated with the compiled value.

Action:

Compile again, giving the new value to `compile(…, model_parameter_list = list(name = value))`.

## The recipe has several algorithms (…): choose one with algorithm = "..."

Action:

Give the name of the algorithm section to run: `MCMC(recipe, algorithm = "mcmc")` (section \@ref(algorithm-sections)).
